notes.1a: The majority of candidates answered this correctly.
notes.1b: Many candidates made vague comments about temperature and volume of ethanol, without using the information given in the question or appreciating how these measurements would be obtained.
notes.1c: Answers were expressed poorly for this question. Many stated that the temperature would decrease, when they clearly meant that the increase would be less.
notes.1d: Most candidates knew that copper was a better conductor of heat than glass. Often this was expressed as the idea that less heat would be lost or that the temperature rise would be greater; both of which were accepted.
notes.2a: Nitric acid was correctly identified by the majority of candidates.
notes.2b: Spatula and stirring rod were both well known, although a significant minority explained why the process was needed rather than what apparatus was used.
notes.2c: Nearly everyone knew that the process was filtration, although crystallisation and evaporation were often seen. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0620 Chemistry June 2015 (d) Candidates found this question challenging. Whilst most said what would remain in the evaporating basin; many could not go on to explain how pure, dry crystals could be obtained, partly because many thought that the original process would achieve that.
notes.4f: The table of results was often completed correctly. A few recorded times in minutes and seconds.
notes.4g: This was also well answered, with the majority correctly drawing a smooth curve. A few joined the points with straight lines. (h) Most could deduce the time for 25 cm , although fewer could sketch the correct curve for a lower temperature. It was either missed altogether or drawn below the original.
notes.4gi: This was well answered, with a large majority identifying the first experiment and stating that it was because the sodium thiosulfate was the most concentrated.
notes.4j: A minority of candidates answered that changing the total volume would make the test unfair. Whilst many did realise that the total volume would no longer be 60 cm , few went on to mention that it would make a comparison with the other results invalid. Common incorrect answers discussed overflow and the size of the measuring cylinder.
notes.4k: Most understood that using a burette as a measuring device would be more accurate. A few good responses compared it to the use of a measuring cylinder or went on to mention that the time taken to add the solution from a burette would make the timing of the experiment less accurate. In the second part, many candidates treated the 100 cm conical flask as another measuring device, rather than a container for the reaction that would give a greater depth of solution and therefore a shorter time.
notes.5b: The most common correct response was the colour of the indicator paper, with fewer mentioning the pungent odour. Many candidates gave the pH or identified the gas as ammonia, but these are not observations.
notes.5c: The correct answer, a yellow precipitate, was seen often, but with a significant number of white precipitates.
notes.5e: Most realised that the pH would be above 7.
notes.5f: Carbon dioxide was correctly identified as the gas by most candidates. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0620 Chemistry June 2015 (g) Many candidates realised that it was a carbonate, with many also correctly identifying the cation as barium, calcium, lead or silver.
notes.6a: Platinum was rarely seen. Carbon or graphite was the most common, incorrect answer.
notes.6b: A number of candidates realised that hydrogen ions have a positive charge.
notes.6c: Chlorine was commonly identified as the gas, with a correct test being given.
notes.6d: Few candidates realised that chlorine is slightly soluble in water.
